names.name: Hanging at the door
names.said: put where everyone entering passes it

text.what: Putting the charm on the way in. A parchment case screwed to a doorpost, a horseshoe nailed above a door, a woven cross in the rafters, a painted star on a barn, a paper talisman pasted at an entrance. The position is the argument: harm is treated as something that arrives, and the door is where it arrives.
text.story:
Jewish law makes the door a legal obligation with a measured position. A mezuzah's parchment goes in a case on the right side of the doorway, in the upper third of the post, at roughly shoulder height and within about three inches — eight centimetres — of the opening. Many Ashkenazi Jews tilt it so that the top slants into the room, a compromise proposed by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, c. 1269–1343, between Rashi's vertical and Rabbeinu Tam's horizontal; most Sephardi, Mizrahi and other non-Ashkenazi Jews fix it vertically. In the diaspora it goes up within thirty days of moving into a rented home; in a purchased home, or anywhere in Israel, immediately. The person holds it to the spot and recites a blessing, and one blessing covers all the doors done in a session. Samaritans set select verses above the house door or on a prominent wall, and stone plaques of the Ten Commandments from the Byzantine and Early Muslim periods, the fourth to the eleventh centuries, are now in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

The door is also where the practice gets litigated. A Chicago condominium association at Shoreline Towers banned objects outside unit doors and in 2004 read the ban as absolute, and management removed residents' mezuzot; complaints went to the Chicago Commission on Human Relations, the Illinois Attorney General and the federal housing department. Alderman Burton Natarus drafted an amendment making it illegal to prohibit a religious sign, symbol or relic on a door, doorpost or entrance, and it became Chicago law that December with a maximum $500 fine, the first such legislation in North America.

Japan assigns doors by deity. Protective gofu such as Tsuno Daishi, the Horned Great Master — the Tendai monk Ryōgen drawn as a yaksha or an oni — go on doorways and entrances; hearth deities go in the kitchen; a talisman of Ucchuṣma, the wrathful figure who purifies the unclean, may go in the toilet. Europe nails iron. Worn horseshoes were placed above or beside doorways to guard houses, barns and stables across Italy, Germany, Britain and Scandinavia, traditionally held with seven nails; whether the ends point up or down is a live disagreement, with much of Europe, the Middle East and Latin America hanging them downward so that blessing pours out, and parts of Ireland and Britain hanging them upward so that luck is caught and cannot run out. The two habits travelled to the United States with their carriers. A legend attached to the tenth-century blacksmith-saint Dunstan has the Devil promising never to enter a household with a horseshoe nailed to the door.

Ireland hangs a woven cross. Saint Brigid's crosses are typically woven on 1 February, and hanging one from the rafters, or over an entryway, was held to bring the saint's blessing and protection for the rest of the year; on the feast day crosses went up in the main dwelling, the outhouses and the stables. Pennsylvania painted the wall instead of the door: barn stars in circular borders appear on Pennsylvania Dutch barns in Berks, Lancaster and Lehigh counties, beginning in the early nineteenth century and spreading once ready-mixed paint became affordable. Two readings of the barn signs run side by side in the same communities — one holds them protective, the other decorative — and both sides agree that particular designs carry folk beliefs. The Amish do not use them.

*Inference —* the door is the most crowded position in this atlas. It is also the only one where the charm is aimed at people who are not its owner: a doorpost charm is read by every visitor, which makes it a statement of who lives here as much as a guard.
text.how: Fix, nail, paste or hang, at the position the tradition specifies, often with words said at the moment of fixing. Height, side and orientation carry rules; so does the date, in the Irish case.
text.today: Live and legally protected in at least one American city. Mezuzot are fixed in Israel and across the diaspora, with cases made in silver, wood, stone, ceramic, pewter and polymer clay; a case sold with a photocopied paper text is a case, since a valid mezuzah is handwritten on parchment by a qualified scribe. Japanese households renew door talismans at the New Year. Hex signs are sold as mountable boards for barns and houses, a trade Jacob Zook of Paradise, Pennsylvania claimed to have started in 1942 for shops along the Lincoln Highway.

dating.label: c. 4th century CE to now
dating.note: Dated from surviving Samaritan stone plaques set above house doors in the Byzantine (4th–7th century) and Early Muslim (7th–11th century) periods, now in the Israel Museum. The biblical command to write on the doorposts is older than any object cited here.

object.note: The eight-centimetre placement figure is the halakhic rule quoted in the cited account, not a measurement of an object.

kin_in.as: where it goes: the rafters, the entryway, the outhouse and the stable

kin_in.name: Bujeok
kin_in.as: the half of its use that never leaves the house, pasted to an interior wall after a gut

kin_in.name: Dol hareubang
kin_in.as: the practice at its heaviest: a doorway guard weighing more than the door
kin_in.name_th: ทลฮารึบัง (รูปปู่หิน)

kin_in.name: Gorgoneion
kin_in.as: the practice the temple antefix is the monumental form of — put the guard where the thing gets in
kin_in.name_th: กอร์โกเนออน (ศีรษะกอร์กอน)

kin_in.name: Hex sign
kin_in.as: the practice it is the biggest version of: a sign fixed to a building, facing outward, in public
kin_in.name_th: เฮ็กซ์ไซน์ (ป้ายดาวบนโรงนา)

kin_in.name: Horseshoe
kin_in.as: the practice in its plainest form, and the one this atlas has the longest argument about direction in
kin_in.name_th: เกือกม้า

kin_in.name: Jimat
kin_in.as: the practice the Indonesian definition leads with: hung on a body, a vehicle or a building
kin_in.name_th: จิมัต (เครื่องรางมลายู)

kin_in.name: Lamashtu plaque
kin_in.as: where these went — beds, doorways, and the places a household counted as open
kin_in.name_th: แผ่นเครื่องรางลามัชตู

kin_in.name: Mezuzah
kin_in.as: the practice, in the atlas's most legally defined form — right post, upper third, eight centimetres from the opening
kin_in.name_th: เมซูซา

kin_in.name: Nimbu mirchi
kin_in.as: the practice this object is: a charm that guards a threshold instead of a person
kin_in.name_th: นิมบู มีร์ชี (มะนาวกับพริก)

kin_in.name: Ofuda
kin_in.as: where half of them end up — gate, doorway, kitchen, ceiling, one per job

kin_in.name: Omikuji
kin_in.as: the nearest practice in this atlas to knotting a fortune onto a pine: a paper fixed in place to do its work where it hangs
kin_in.name_th: โอมิกุจิ (ใบเซียมซีญี่ปุ่น)

kin_in.name: Pazuzu head
kin_in.as: the practice the Dur-Katlimmu find caught in the act — hung on the wall facing the entryway
kin_in.name_th: เศียรปาซูซู

kin_in.name: Rowan cross
kin_in.as: where it mostly went: over a door, over a byre lintel, above a hearth
kin_in.name_th: กางเขนไม้โรวัน

kin_in.name: Teru teru bōzu
kin_in.as: where it works from — an eave, a window frame, outside, where the weather can see it
kin_in.name_th: เทรุเทรุโบซุ (ตุ๊กตาไล่ฝน)

kin_in.name: Fulu — Taoist talismanic craft

kin_in.name: Bujeok craft
kin_in.as: the practice, done indoors: the talisman goes on the inside wall of the house it is for
kin_in.name_th: บูจ็อก (ศาสตร์ยันต์เกาหลี)

kin_in.name: Mesopotamian household protection
kin_in.as: the practice this tradition is built on: put the guard where the thing gets in
kin_in.name_th: การคุ้มครองบ้านเรือนแบบเมโสโปเตเมีย

kin_in.name: The bell
kin_in.as: the practice the Roman half of this record belongs to entirely
kin_in.name_th: กระดิ่ง

kin_in.name: The key
kin_in.as: the practice this sign points at, even where no key is actually hung
kin_in.name_th: กุญแจ

kin_in.name: The mirror
kin_in.as: the practice the bagua mirror belongs to, and the one that makes it a neighbour's problem
kin_in.name_th: กระจก

kin_in.name: The serpent
kin_in.as: the practice the guardian snake belongs to, in stone rather than in metal
kin_in.name_th: งู

kin_in.name: The tree
kin_in.as: the practice the rowan belongs to: the sign is placed at the threshold, not worn
kin_in.name_th: ต้นไม้

kin_in.name: Iron
kin_in.as: the practice iron is most often put to — over the lintel, under the threshold, around the graveyard
kin_in.name_th: เหล็ก

kin_in.name: Salt
kin_in.as: where salt is most often put: a threshold, a gate, a shop entrance
kin_in.name_th: เกลือ

kin_in.name: fu
kin_in.as: the practice the fortune character exists for: paper, paste, doorpost, once a year
kin_in.name_th: ฝู (福)

kin_in.name: ward
kin_in.as: the practice the verb is nearly always attached to in English writing
kin_in.name_th: วอร์ด (ปัดเป่า)

kin_in.name: The charm in the wall
kin_in.as: the visible answer to the same fear: the horseshoe over the door, where the bottle goes under it
kin_in.name_th: เครื่องรางในกำแพง
